---
title: "Sequential surveillance with MaxSPRT"
subtitle: "Critical values, calibrated LLRs, and a worked pipeline"
---

The theory is on the [MaxSPRT](../methods/maxsprt.qmd) page. This one runs an
analysis.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import empiricalcalibration as ec
```

## Critical values

The threshold depends on the schedule of looks, expressed as the expected number
of events under the null in each group.

```{python}
#| warning: false
groupSizes = [1.0] * 10          # ten looks, one expected event each

ec.set_seed(1)
cv = ec.computeCvPoisson(groupSizes, alpha=0.05, sampleSize=10_000)
print(f"critical value: {float(cv):.4f}")
print(f"alpha achieved: {cv.alpha}")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Read `cv.alpha`, always

There is usually no critical value that hits the requested alpha exactly. These
functions pick the least conservative value whose realised alpha is still below
what you asked for, and report it. At `sampleSize=10_000` the granularity is
coarse; at the default 1,000,000 it is fine.
:::

For a binomial (self-controlled or matched) design, supply `z` — the ratio of
control to exposed, so the null probability is $p = 1/(1+z)$:

```{python}
#| warning: false
ec.set_seed(2)
cv_binom = ec.computeCvBinomial(groupSizes, z=4, sampleSize=10_000)
print(f"binomial CV: {float(cv_binom):.4f}  (alpha {cv_binom.alpha})")
```

And for a Poisson regression design with a control window:

```{python}
#| warning: false
ec.set_seed(3)
cv_reg = ec.computeCvPoissonRegression(groupSizes, z=4, sampleSize=10_000)
print(f"Poisson regression CV: {float(cv_reg):.4f}  (alpha {cv_reg.alpha})")
```

### Accounting for systematic error in the threshold

Pass `nullMean` and `nullSd` from a fitted empirical null, and each simulated
trial draws its own systematic error rather than assuming none:

```{python}
#| warning: false
sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)

ec.set_seed(1)
cv_cal = ec.computeCvPoisson(groupSizes, sampleSize=10_000,
                             nullMean=null[0], nullSd=null[1])

print(f"uncalibrated CV: {float(cv):.3f}")
print(f"calibrated CV:   {float(cv_cal):.3f}")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Budget the runtime

The examples here use `sampleSize=10_000` so this page renders quickly. The
default is 1,000,000 and takes seconds to tens of seconds per call. Use the
default for anything you report — the Monte-Carlo error in the critical value is
part of your error budget, and 10,000 samples is not enough to pin a 95%
quantile.
:::

## Calibrating the statistic

`calibrateLlr` takes the null and a likelihood approximation for the estimate
under test.

```{python}
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]
llr = ec.calibrateLlr(null, positive)
print("calibrated LLR:", llr[0], " -> signal?", bool(llr[0] > float(cv_cal)))
```

Zero: once the design's demonstrated systematic error is accounted for, this
estimate carries no evidence against the null.

With grid likelihood profiles instead of normal approximations — the right
choice when event counts are small:

```{python}
from empiricalcalibration._rmath import dnorm

ec.set_seed(123)
sim = ec.simulateControls(n=50, mean=0.2, sd=0.2, trueLogRr=0, seLogRr=0.1)
point = np.linspace(np.log(0.1), np.log(10), 1000)
profiles = [
    pd.DataFrame({"point": point,
                  "value": dnorm(point, sim.logRr.iloc[i], sim.seLogRr.iloc[i])})
    for i in range(len(sim))
]

grid_null = ec.fitNullNonNormalLl(profiles)
ec.calibrateLlr(grid_null, profiles[:5]).round(4)
```

## A full pipeline on simulated data

`simulateMaxSprtData` produces a multi-look dataset with negative controls, a
positive control, and a systematic error built in.

```{python}
ec.set_seed(42)
data = ec.simulateMaxSprtData(
    n=10_000,
    numberOfNegativeControls=20,
    numberOfPositiveControls=1,
    looks=10,
)
data.head()
```

Compute a per-look, per-outcome Poisson rate ratio against unexposed time, then
run the calibration at the final look.

```{python}
def estimate_at_look(df, look):
    """Crude Poisson rate-ratio estimate per outcome at a given look."""
    d = df[df.lookTime == look]
    rows = []
    for outcome_id, g in d.groupby("outcomeId"):
        exposed = g[g.exposure == 1]
        unexposed = g[g.exposure == 0]
        a, b = exposed.outcome.sum(), unexposed.outcome.sum()
        t1, t0 = exposed.time.sum(), unexposed.time.sum()
        if a == 0 or b == 0:
            rows.append((outcome_id, np.nan, np.nan))
            continue
        logRr = np.log((a / t1) / (b / t0))
        seLogRr = np.sqrt(1 / a + 1 / b)
        rows.append((outcome_id, logRr, seLogRr))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["outcomeId", "logRr", "seLogRr"])

final_look = sorted(data.lookTime.unique())[-1]
est = estimate_at_look(data, final_look).dropna()
est.head()
```

```{python}
# Outcome IDs are assigned negative controls first, so the positive control
# takes the highest ID.
positive_id = est.outcomeId.max()
neg_est = est[est.outcomeId != positive_id]
pos_est = est[est.outcomeId == positive_id]

sim_null = ec.fitNull(neg_est.logRr, neg_est.seLogRr)
print(sim_null)
print()
print("EASE:", round(float(ec.computeExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError(sim_null)), 3))
```

```{python}
#| warning: false
llr_cal = ec.calibrateLlr(sim_null, pos_est[["logRr", "seLogRr"]])

ec.set_seed(9)
cv_final = ec.computeCvPoisson([1.0] * 10, sampleSize=10_000,
                               nullMean=sim_null[0], nullSd=sim_null[1])

print(f"calibrated LLR : {llr_cal[0]:.3f}")
print(f"critical value : {float(cv_final):.3f}")
print(f"signal         : {bool(llr_cal[0] > float(cv_final))}")
```

## Choosing a design by EASE

When several designs are available, run each on the same negative controls and
prefer the one with least systematic error — see
[EASE](../methods/ease.qmd#comparing-two-designs) for the paired comparison that
respects the shared controls.

```python
result = ec.compareEase(designA.logRr, designA.seLogRr,
                        designB.logRr, designB.seLogRr)
```
